ns2:section.sectionText: This course invites reflection on what we do when we read and write about literature. Is there something distinctive about literary language and the experience of reading literary texts? What is the difference between a newspaper narrative and a short story? How do we compare different interpretations of a poem? Does the study of literature have any relevance outside the academy? English 301 explores these and related questions and considers some of the most influential responses they have received in the last seventy years or so, from critical schools including the New Criticism, feminism, Marxism, deconstruction, psychoanalysis, postcolonialism, the New Historicism, and the new formalisms. The course prepares you to engage, more thoughtfully, the scholarship that you draw upon when you write research papers for literature classes. It also gives you the tools to articulate and defend your own interpretive approach to literature and culture. It is strongly recommended that all English and Teaching of English majors take ENGL 300 and ENGL 301 BEFORE taking any other 300- or 400-level courses.
